q: Why does the RefSeq-PGAP transposase count (458 for CBW1002, 340 for CBW1006) differ by ~8x from the paper's BGI-RAST count (59, 35)? Is PGAP over-splitting IS elements into pseudogene fragments, or is BGI under-annotating?
basis: Our RefSeq PGAP re-annotation gave 458/340 transposase-labeled CDS vs paper's 59/35. Ratio direction is preserved (CBW1002 > CBW1006) but absolute counts diverge 8x.
next_steps: Direct locus-level comparison of the two GFF annotations for CBW1002 (BGI-RAST vs PGAP), classify per-family IS content with ISfinder to determine which pipeline is closer to the biological truth.

q: Is the Bornholm Sea cluster placement of CBW1002/CBW1006 robust to using multi-locus concatenated markers (rpoC1, ITS) instead of 16S alone, and to adding more Baltic Sea genomes?
basis: Our 16S phylogeny places CBW1002/1006 closest to Cyanobium_gracile_PCC6307 (97.85% ID) rather than to the only publicly-available Bornholm reference BS55D (97.10% ID). BS55D itself groups with WH8102 (marine 5.1) in our tree, not with CBW.
next_steps: Sequence 2-3 additional Baltic Sea Synechococcus isolates (BS4, BS5, BS7 - only partial 16S clones available currently), then rebuild the phylogeny using rpoC1+ITS+16S concatenated matrix.

q: Does the paper's GC-content number (>65%) come from the original BGI assembly (potentially pre-polishing) or from a calculation including N-bases, given that our strict A/T/G/C computation on the deposited RefSeq FASTA gives 64.64% and 64.57%?
basis: Both genomes report identically ~0.5pp lower GC than the paper on the FINAL deposited sequence, and both show 0 Ns in the assembly. The systematic 0.5pp offset suggests a formula difference, not a base-count difference.
next_steps: Recompute GC using multiple canonical definitions (SeqKit stats, BioPython GC123, EMBOSS geecee) on the RefSeq FASTA; also request the BGI raw-assembly FASTA from the corresponding author to check whether pre-polish GC differed.

q: Given that neither CBW1002 nor CBW1006 encodes canonical bacterial cold-shock proteins (cspA/B/C/G) yet both grow at 4-10 C, what is the actual cold-response transcriptome? Are the many desaturase and chaperone genes sufficient, or are there novel unannotated cold-shock analogs?
basis: Confirmed 0 cspA/B/C/G annotations in both PGAP-annotated genomes - the paper's most surprising biological claim. The paper points to desaturases and chaperones as the alternative but does not test this experimentally.
next_steps: RNA-seq CBW1002 grown at 4 C vs 20 C for 2 hours (both mid-log); look for differentially-expressed 'unknown function' genes among the 3,023 CBW-shared homologs that are up-regulated in cold, especially small (<100 aa) proteins that may be novel cold-response factors.

q: CBW1002 has ~35% more annotated transposase copies than CBW1006 in both annotation pipelines, yet the two genomes are only 6 kbp different in total length and share 2,949 RBH proteins. Where are the extra transposases physically located, and are they in a few high-copy IS families or scattered genome-wide?
basis: Consistent CBW1002 > CBW1006 direction in both BGI-RAST (59 vs 35) and PGAP (458 vs 340) suggests real biological asymmetry, but the paper does not describe the physical distribution.
next_steps: Classify all CBW1002 and CBW1006 transposase CDS by ISfinder IS family, produce a linear IS-content map, and run a synteny dotplot (nucmer/D-GENIES) between the two chromosomes to reveal whether the extra IS load in CBW1002 is one big cluster or many small insertions.
